text:
As long as one Black child was left in town, the school had to stay open. That is how her son remembered the rule, and she stayed. The families were being hauled twenty-five miles out of the county, and as the roll fell she became the principal, then the janitor, then whatever else the building needed that morning, ten children, then nine, then eight, still unlocking that door on her own. Sit with that a second, and then sit with this: in her own son's account of everything she did, she is never once given a name.

The town was Sheridan, Arkansas, and it had started out voting the other way. On the twenty-first of May 1954, four days after the Supreme Court struck down school segregation, five men on the Sheridan School Board voted five to nothing to seat twenty-one Black students alongside about six hundred white students that September.

Twenty-four hours later the same five men voted five to nothing to take it back.

The town that did it sits thirty-four miles south of Little Rock, county seat of Grant County, in the pine of the Arkansas timberlands. The county was named for Ulysses S. Grant and the town for Philip Sheridan by Union men after the war, and residents tried more than once over the years to get both names changed and never managed it.

The board had not arrived at that first vote on its own. Southern School News, the trade paper that tracked every southern district week by week, reported in September 1954 that Sheridan had acted while facing protests from Black residents over unequal facilities.

The parents had complained. Sheridan's Black community was not sitting quietly waiting to be acted upon, and the vote that started all of this was something they had pushed for and won.

They had the state behind them too, for about a week. Three days before the vote, on the eighteenth of May, Governor Francis Cherry said that "Arkansas will obey the law," and added that it always had.

So the board had cover from the governor and a grievance in front of it, and it moved. Black pupils would go into the upper six grades in the fall, and Lambert Wing School, the two-room building the Black community used, would keep the younger children.

The protests from white patrons started immediately. The board met the next evening and rescinded the whole thing, unanimously, the way it had passed it.

Rescinding it did not settle the town. On the first of June about three hundred patrons of the Sheridan district met and instructed a committee to circulate petitions demanding that the entire board resign.

On the seventh of June a board member named Russell Hendon resigned, and the contemporary account records no reason given for it. The historian John A. Kirk records four members ultimately leaving their seats over a vote they had already reversed.

What the board had left to work out was what the reversal would cost. On the twenty-eighth of July, Superintendent A. R. McKenzie set out the plan.

Eleven of the twenty-one students would be carried by bus every day to a high school twenty-seven miles away in an adjoining county. He put the tuition and transportation at four thousand dollars a year, on top of an initial four thousand dollars to buy the bus.

Eight thousand dollars in the first year. For eleven children, to keep them out of a building they had already been voted into.

The other ten, the seventh and eighth graders, would stay at the Black school in Sheridan. They would be taught, McKenzie said, by the same two Black teachers who had covered grades one through twelve the year before.

Two teachers covering twelve grades. That was the separate half of separate but equal in Grant County, Arkansas, and it is the exact complaint the parents had carried to the board in the first place.

Another Arkansas board voted on the very same day. Fayetteville, up in the northwest corner, announced that it would seat nine Black students with about five hundred whites in its high school, and Southern School News reported that it did so primarily for financial reasons.

The district had been sending those nine to Fort Smith, sixty miles off, and Hot Springs, a hundred and fifty miles off, at a cost of around five thousand dollars the previous year. Fayetteville's superintendent later said that no more than four patrons had spoken to him bitterly about the decision.

The board received about forty letters, all of them favorable except one, and that one came from someone who did not live in the state.

So the town that acted on money was Fayetteville, and it held. The town that acted because Black parents pressed it was Sheridan, and it broke within twenty-four hours.

The Fayetteville children who walked in that fall can still be traced. Photographs of the district's Black students from those first years survive with names attached, printed under the picture, rows of teenagers looking at the camera.

The published record does not carry a roll of Sheridan's twenty-one. That absence is not proof the names were never written down anywhere, only that nobody has published them.

Those twenty-one children came out of a community barely thirty years old. There had been almost no Black families in Grant County until the 1920s, when the forest industries came in and needed hands.

By the early fifties there were about a hundred and ninety-nine Black residents in a town of eighteen hundred and ninety-eight. For years the only schooling their children got came from Melissa Dorn, the wife of a Baptist minister named Henry Dorn.

She taught them herself, in the way Black women across the South taught children when the county would not.

In the fall of 1936 another minister, a Reverend Nall, pushed the parents to organize and walk into the Sheridan School Board together and ask for a teacher. The board hired one.

When the school year opened that October, thirteen children enrolled. They met inside Stranger's Rest Baptist Church, in the Black neighborhood pressed up against the J. L. Williams and Sons mill.

Two years later somebody photographed that class. It is a black and white print, five inches by seven, and it shows a woman named Rubeye Nichols Lambert standing with her students at the church that was serving as their school.

The catalogue entry at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, where the print is held in the African Americans photograph collection, dates it to 1938 and calls the children the Lambert Wing group. There was no Lambert Wing building in 1938.

The building came in 1940, one room, and it took its name from them. The name belonged to a teacher and a set of children before it ever belonged to a structure.

A second room and two more teachers arrived in 1951 and 1952. That was the entire educational estate of Black Sheridan, and its name had started as a woman's.

In 1936 the parents of that neighborhood organized and went to the school board and got a teacher. In 1954 they organized and went to the school board and got a vote.

Both times they won. The second time, the town's answer was to get rid of them.

The town had already shown what it was willing to do. A Black man named Amos Neely was lynched in Sheridan in 1898, and a Black man named Ed McCollum was killed there in 1903, both over allegations of assault.

On the nineteenth of January 1922 the Sheridan newspaper announced that the Ku Klux Klan had organized in Grant County and noted that nobody knew who the members were or where they met. A Klan parade followed through the streets of Sheridan, which the county's own reference entries date to the March of either 1922 or 1923 and number at somewhere between fifty-five and a hundred and fifty-five men.

So when the board reversed itself in the spring of 1954, nobody in Sheridan needed the alternative explained. What actually happened next has no mob in it at all.

J. L. Williams and Sons had set up in Sheridan in 1923, and by 1954 the mill was the town. It employed most of the Black families in the county and it owned the houses those families slept in, in the neighborhood alongside the yard.

That is what a company town means when it is turned against you. One man holds your wages and your roof, and he can move one of them without laying a finger on the other.

The state's own encyclopedia tells what happened next three separate times, in three separate entries, and it does not tell it the same way twice.

The entry on the town of Sheridan calls it a "family relocation plan" and says many of the details are not known. It reports that the mill told its Black employees that the land under the company housing was needed for mill expansion, that they would keep their jobs, and that they could take the houses outright provided the houses were moved out of the area, with the mill helping toward the cost.

The entry on sundown towns, written by the historian James Loewen, records something harder. The mill's owner, Jack Williams, offered to give the families their houses and move them twenty-five miles west to Malvern at no cost, and told them that a family refusing the arrangement would be evicted and would watch its house burn.

The entry on Grant County splits the difference and does not soften the verb. It says the Black population of Sheridan was essentially evicted, and that the choice put to them was the houses and the move, or forcible eviction.

One reference work, three entries, three tellings. That is what a town's memory looks like while the town is still deciding what it is prepared to have written down.

What none of them dispute is where the houses went. Twenty-five miles west, out of Grant County, into Hot Spring County and the town of Malvern.

The Black people in Sheridan who did not work for the mill, the preachers and the men and women running their own small businesses, found within weeks that their congregations and their customers had been moved twenty-five miles down the road.

You do not have to evict a barber. You only have to move everyone who was getting a haircut.

They left too. Sheridan did bus students out of the county that autumn, and every year after there were fewer of them to carry.

The plan had been drawn for eleven children and the removal kept subtracting from it. Sheridan settled what the Supreme Court had handed it without one arrest, one shot fired, or one line in the paper about race.

J. L. Williams and Sons, which needed that land for expansion in 1954, was gone from Sheridan by the 1960s.

This is the machinery of a sundown town, and it is not what most people picture when they hear the phrase. Loewen's central finding, after years of counting, was that white southerners rarely bothered with expulsion, because the South had other ways of holding Black people in place, and that the driving out was largely a northern and midwestern habit.

He went looking expecting perhaps fifty of these places in the whole country. He found more than five hundred in Illinois alone and came to estimate around ten thousand nationally at their peak in 1970.

Arkansas sat on the seam and ran probably more than a hundred of them across the northwestern two thirds of the state.

In 1890 every single county in Arkansas had at least six Black residents, and only one had fewer than ten. By 1960 six counties had none at all, Baxter, Fulton, Polk, Searcy, Sharp and Stone, and seven more were down to one, two or three people.

Those are counties, and Sheridan is a town. What Sheridan did in 1954 it did by contract rather than by mob, and the neighborhood beside the mill came apart house by house.

All the while, the school stayed open. Arkansas statute required every district in the state to run separate schools for white and Black children.

James Seawood, who was a boy in that neighborhood, remembered how that worked in practice: one Black child left in town was enough to keep the doors open. So the only way for Sheridan to end the obligation was to end the children.

The school and the neighborhood emptied at the same rate. Seawood used to climb the stacked lumber in the mill yard and stand on top of it to look across at the white school.

He could see the size of it from up there, the band, the football team, the whole apparatus of an American childhood laid out in front of a boy standing on a woodpile.

Then he would climb down and walk back to two rooms and outdoor toilets. The mill he had been standing on was the same mill that was moving his neighbors twenty-five miles west.

His mother stayed on alone. There is no version of this in which somebody arrives to help her.

She unlocked the door for eight. She unlocked it for five, and for three, and she kept unlocking it for as long as there was one child left in town to unlock it for.

The high school students who were left had been put on a bus out of the county. The contemporary plan named a school twenty-seven miles off in an adjoining county, while the Encyclopedia of Arkansas records them being carried that fall to Pine Bluff, which is further, and the two accounts have never been reconciled.

By 1961 every Black family had gone from the Sheridan area and Lambert Wing closed. Then word reached his mother that the building was coming down.

She and her son got into the old station wagon and drove over there. They went inside and gathered up whatever records they could find, the paper history of every child who had passed through those two rooms, and carried it out by the armful and put it in the back of the wagon.

That is one woman and one boy loading a school into a car. Nobody sent an archivist and nobody offered a box.

Then a bulldozer came and dug a hole. It pushed the school into the hole and covered it over, and afterward there was nothing on that ground to show a school had ever stood there.

Not knocked down and carted off, with the lot cleared and sold. Dug under, and the dirt raked level over the top of it.

Whatever reason anybody gave for doing it that way, the result was the same. The building did not close, it went into the ground.

Years later, sitting in graduate school classes where urban renewal was discussed as a planning question, Seawood had his own definition ready. Urban renewal was a deep hole with your school in it, filled in until it looked as though neither the school nor the people who went to it had ever existed.

The school district kept almost nothing. Its board minutes do not mention Lambert Wing again until March 1957, and the surviving school records carry no other reference to the school or to the Supreme Court decision that set every bit of this in motion.

That silence is not carelessness. Loewen's finding, after years of this work, is that sundown towns are difficult to research precisely because the communities took care that nothing about the policy was ever written down.

In 1973 the sociologist Gordon Morgan, trying to reconstruct Black life in the Arkansas Ozarks, wrote that some white towns had deliberately destroyed the reminders of the Black people who once lived there. He was describing a region, not a town.

There was a schoolhouse lying under a field in Grant County that fit his sentence exactly. He had no way of knowing it was there.

Sheridan's schools did eventually take Black students again, and even that date is disputed inside the same encyclopedia. One entry puts it in the mid-1980s, when consolidation folded in students from two small biracial communities nearby, and another says the schools stayed all white until 1992, when consolidation brought in the first Black students.

Somewhere between thirty and thirty-eight years, then. And in neither version did the town reverse itself, because in both versions what changed was where the district lines ran.

Around 1995 a Black family moved into Sheridan. Before the decade was out, three more had joined them.

Four families. Roughly forty years after the mill emptied the neighborhood, four families.

Sheridan started with a hundred and ninety-nine Black residents in a town of eighteen hundred and ninety-eight. In the 2000 census, out of 3,872 people, fewer than one in a hundred were Black.

What is left of that community is not much. The school is under a field and the board minutes say nothing.

The houses went to Malvern, and nobody has published a list of which ones or who was riding behind them.

But that photograph exists. Five inches by seven, black and white, held in the African Americans photograph collection at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, catalogued and online, and in it Rubeye Nichols Lambert is standing with the children of a school a town later buried.

Her name is on the record. So is the name of the school, which was her name, which is the one part of that building the bulldozer could not reach.

And the woman who stayed on alone until the last child was gone is identified in Seawood's StoryCorps account only as his mother. That recording preserves everything she did and none of what she was called.

When this story comes up in front of you, give it the county and give it the year, and add the two parts that always fall off. The parents asked for it first, and the school had a principal and a janitor and they were the same woman.

And if anybody in your own family came out of a town that emptied, ask them the year and ask them the name of the school while there is still somebody in the room to ask.

James Seawood said his hometown was still an all-white town. Then he told anybody who ever got the chance to pass through it to "drive very slowly."

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

• Today: US cash reopens, Canada's tariffs bite, Nektar's jury trial against Eli Lilly opens, Beam Therapeutics presents its alpha-1 gene editing data at ERS in Barcelona this morning. Casey's, Braze and ServiceTitan after the close.
• Wednesday: 10Y auction, the first four-billion-dollar long-bond buyback, Chewy and Signet before the open. Thursday: PPI, existing home sales, the second buyback, then Oracle and Adobe after the close, the two prints that decide whether software's liquidation is over.
• Friday: CPI at 14:30 CEST, the print the Fed's swing votes have named. Michigan expectations alongside it.
• Next week: FOMC on the 15th and 16th with projections and a press conference, quarterly expiry and the S&P rebalance on the 18th, effective the 21st. Anthropic's public filing is reported for this week, unverified.

🧠 BOTTOM LINE
• Two shocks landed overnight and they point the same way for rates. The Saudi attacks put two and a half percent on crude and the BoJ report put a hike into the last major central bank still at emergency settings. Both are inflation news. Both push real yields up, which is what the TIPS curve did and what gold is paying for this morning.
• The bond market has had the worst decade in its recorded history and the ten-year is sitting at its high of the year going into the last inflation prints before a live Fed meeting. Whether Friday's CPI is hot or cold, the long end is not going to be the safe haven in either outcome; it stopped being one in 2020 and the numbers now say so.
• Equities are splitting again rather than falling. Semis and Micron bid, financials and gold offered, Oracle up four percent into its print. That is the dispersion regime of the last two weeks continuing, and it rewards being right on the name rather than the index.
• The AI trade got its confirmation from two directions in one morning: capability rose at flat prices across three labs in a week, and the physical spend behind it rose 57%. The names that sell the capacity are the ones the market is buying pre-market.
• The risk into Friday is not the print, it is the yen. A Japanese hike with the Nikkei already down 1.7% is the funding leg of the world's carry trade tightening in the week the Fed decides. Korea and the leveraged Asian tech complex felt it first; if it spreads, it does so through the highest-beta longs.

🇺🇸 VA — An excellent benefit for eligible Veterans, service members and certain surviving spouses. VA loans can offer 0% down, competitive rates and no private mortgage insurance (PMI).

text:
TELANGANA SEEKS TO INCREASE RICE EXPORTS AND TRADE WITH THE PHILIPPINES – UTTAM

Telangana Minister for Irrigation and Food & Civil Supplies Capt. N. Uttam Kumar Reddy met Mr. Francisco P. Tu Laurel Jr., Secretary of Agriculture of the Republic of the Philippines and a member of the Philippine Cabinet, in New Delhi on Tuesday. (Mr. Francisco P. Tu Laurel Jr.’s position in Philippines is equivalent in India to that of a Union Cabinet Minister responsible for irrigation, agriculture and food.)

The two leaders held detailed discussions on the possibility of increasing rice exports and also increasing trade between Telangana and Philippines.

Uttam Kumar Reddy explained that Telangana had emerged as one of India’s leading paddy-producing states and possessed the production capacity, modern rice-milling infrastructure and experience required to supply high-quality rice in substantial quantities.

Secretary Laurel responded positively to the proposal and indicated that the Philippines would examine the possibility of sourcing larger quantities of rice from Telangana. The two sides discussed how the proposal could be taken forward through the appropriate government agencies, recognised importers, exporters and rice millers.

The discussions assume importance in view of the Philippines’ substantial requirement for imported rice and its efforts to diversify its international sources of supply. Uttam Kumar Reddy said Telangana could offer competitive prices, dependable quality and timely delivery and could emerge as a trusted long-term supplier of rice to the Philippines.

The meeting also covered rice varieties, quality standards, pricing, procurement mechanisms, logistics, certification procedures and sanitary and phytosanitary requirements. Both sides agreed that officials and industry representatives should examine these issues and prepare a practical roadmap for translating the discussions into concrete trade opportunities.

Secretary Laurel also expressed interest in procuring meat products and quality seeds from Telangana. Uttam Kumar Reddy welcomed the interest and said Telangana had strong capabilities in seed production, food processing and allied agricultural sectors. The available product categories and regulatory requirements would be examined in consultation with the relevant authorities and private-sector representatives.

Uttam Kumar Reddy said expanding agricultural exports would create new opportunities for Telangana’s farmers, rice millers, seed companies, food-processing industries and other participants in the rural economy.

“Our objective is to create dependable and remunerative international markets for Telangana’s farmers and agricultural industries. Telangana has the production capacity, processing infrastructure and entrepreneurial strength to become a reliable long-term supplier of rice and other agricultural products to the Philippines,” he said.

The leaders also discussed a wide range of issues relating to India–Philippines relations, food security, agricultural cooperation and the broader potential for increasing direct trade between Telangana and the Philippines. They observed that agriculture and food trade could become an important component of the growing strategic partnership between India and the Philippines.

Uttam Kumar Reddy and Secretary Laurel extended invitations to each other to visit their respective regions. Uttam Kumar Reddy specially invited Secretary Laurel to visit Hyderabad and participate in the Telangana Rising Summit scheduled to be held in December 2026.

The meeting concluded on a highly positive note, with both sides expressing their commitment to pursue the issues discussed and strengthen cooperation in agriculture, rice and food trade, seed development and related sectors.

“For many gig worker advocates, the reclassification path—reclassify rideshare drivers as employees, and then unionize them—represents the best way forward for organizing. Others have been pursuing a competing strategy. In November 2024, Massachusetts voters passed Question 3, a ballot initiative that extended a unique kind of collective bargaining right to rideshare drivers—without first granting them rights as employees. Similar laws have been recently passed, in California in October 2025 and Illinois in August of this year, and legislation has been introduced in Minnesota. In theory, these new laws offer the possibility of collective representation to enormous numbers of workers: the campaigns claim 70,000 rideshare drivers in Massachusetts, 800,000 in California, and 100,000 in Illinois.

Champions of sectoral bargaining see in these state-level experiments a promising new approach for unions in the twenty-first century. But without closing the hole in minimum wage coverage ripped open by rideshare companies’ exploitation of independent contracting, do these new frameworks in the US suggest organized labor is simply legitimizing the business models of Uber and Lyft?”

US Open ATP 

Frances Tiafoe vs Alex Michelsen

🧠 Form & Context

Frances Tiafoe

🔥 Nine wins from his last ten completed matches: Tiafoe’s recent overall and hard-court records both stand at 9–1. His 84.3 Combined Form Score gives him a substantial advantage over Michelsen’s 67.8.

🎯 A strong response after an extended opening round: Following his five-set match against Martin Damm, Tiafoe completed consecutive straight-set victories over Rei Sakamoto, Valentin Vacherot and Daniil Medvedev. His latest result was 7–6(1), 6–4, 7–6(6).

🏆 Recent success against stronger opposition: Medvedev, Lorenzo Musetti, Félix Auger-Aliassime and Brandon Nakashima all appear among his completed victories across this recent hard-court stretch. His supplied last-52-week record against Top-20 opponents is 9–9.

🧩 Excellent conversion, less dominant underlying control: Tiafoe converts 46.6% of break points, but wins only 21.4% of return games in the supplied statistical table. His results support the favourite’s direction more strongly than they support a comfortable winning margin.

🩼 Durability remains a qualification: The Montreal retirement on 7 August is excluded from completed-match form. Subsequent results provide encouraging evidence of recovery, although the supplied warmer daytime conditions would make another extended contest a meaningful physical test.

Alex Michelsen

✅ Four rounds without dropping a set: Michelsen has completed straight-set victories over Federico Cina, Brandon Nakashima, Daniel Mérida Aguilar and Tomás Martín Etcheverry. He arrives with a 12–0 tournament set record.

📈 His tournament form is stronger than the broader sample: A 7–3 last-ten record produces a lower CFS, but his four most recent performances show a clear improvement in consistency.

👀 The Nakashima victory deserves proper weight: Michelsen beat him 6–3, 6–4, 6–4 in the second round. His run should not be reduced to the Etcheverry result alone.

🔄 A relevant second-serve return threat: Michelsen wins 52.9% of second-serve return points. That creates a plausible pressure point against Tiafoe’s 58.7% first-serve accuracy.

🛡️ A credible service platform: His 84.6% hold rate exceeds Tiafoe’s 81.6% in the supplied table. His 68.2% break-point save rate also suggests he can resist pressure without needing to dominate every service game.

⚠️ The remaining question is opposition level: A 2–9 record against Top-20 opponents over the last 52 weeks limits confidence that this clean tournament run will translate into another victory against a higher-ranked opponent.

🔍 Match Breakdown

Tiafoe has the stronger recent body of work, particularly after adjusting for opposition. His victory over Medvedev provides the clearest immediate evidence: he completed the match in three sets and handled two tiebreaks successfully. Alongside his Cincinnati results, that supports his ability to produce against opponents capable of exposing weaknesses over sustained periods.

However, the 16.5-point CFS advantage is not a 16.5-point advantage in match-winning probability. It describes the difference in the selected form inputs. Michelsen’s superior hold rate and almost identical return-game win rate show why the matchup can remain competitive despite that sizeable form gap.

The second serve is a particularly important interaction. Tiafoe wins 73.9% of first-serve points, but his first-serve accuracy leaves a substantial share of points to be played behind the second delivery. Michelsen’s second-serve returning gives him a route into those games. If Tiafoe repeatedly starts rallies without the advantage of his first serve, the favourite may struggle to establish scoreboard separation.

Tiafoe’s response needs to be efficient first-strike tennis: protect the second serve, take control with the first attacking ball and prevent Michelsen from repeatedly settling into balanced baseline exchanges. His strong break-point conversion is encouraging, although relying on exceptional conversion alone would make the match more fragile than the recent results suggest.

Michelsen’s physical case is also relevant. He has played 12 sets, compared with Tiafoe’s 14. That is a measurable workload difference; actual court-time totals were not supplied. Both completed their previous round on the same date, so Michelsen’s advantage comes from the lighter tournament workload rather than an additional rest day.

The supplied warmer daytime scenario increases the importance of efficiency, but Tiafoe’s retirement history should not be presented as evidence of an active injury. His completed matches since Montreal support a reduced-confidence favourite’s assessment, rather than an assumption that he will fade.

The supplied H2H favours Tiafoe 2–0. The most recent meeting, a 7–5, 6–1 victory in Houston in 2025, offers some supporting context, but its clay surface limits its relevance to this hard-court quarterfinal.

🔮 Prediction

text:
I’m an Israeli. I’ve lived in the UK on and off for the past 20-something years. I met my wife here. I had my children here. I’ve built a life here, contributed more than most to the country, never taken a penny in benefits or anything else, and I find myself truly heartbroken with what this country has become. 

Over the years I’ve been here, I’ve seen the change. It wasn’t slow and gradual. It was fast, shambolic, and corrupt. I’ve watched as good decent British people had their lives changed by those who came here like parasites to feed off the state, and a state all too happy to give those parasites everything while taking more and more from their own people, especially their rights and their dignity. 

But the most painful part for me was watching the good and decent people of this country sit back and do absolutely nothing. 

I’ve asked myself countless times how an entire population could just take it, watch it all unfold in front of them, watch as their own government and media painted them as right wing extremists when all they wanted was peaceful existence and for any foreign visitors to respect their country, their flag, their culture and their way of life. And yet the opposite happened AND THEY DID NOTHING. 

Britain has just made the single biggest mistake with this latest decision against Israel. There is no logic behind it. There is no moral justification for it. But when you’re here and you see the utter corruption of this pathetic government, it all starts to make sense in how they did it. 

Socialism and communism is rife in this government, as is the new plague of Palestinianism and a Muslim revolution. The more the people of this country try speak out and resist it, the more the government crushes them with policy after policy that takes more and more away from them. And yet, they still do nothing about it. 

There will be no redemption from this latest failure of morality. There will be no turning back. And the people for all their talk and the few politicians promising change, nothing will change. Only one side fights. Only one side takes to the street. Only one side has any balls and takes whatever they want. The few protests by the people are simply not enough. They’re so desperate to be seen as good and silent that they don’t realize what they’re even up against. 

But I do. I lived through it, lost family because of it, watch the world turned upside down because of it, and now I watch my adopted home torn apart because of it. It isn’t going to get better. It isn’t going to change. And my priority now is my own children’s futures. This country simply isn’t it. It has nothing left to offer. It’s once great institutions like Cambridge and Oxford are little more than cesspits of socialism and communism and leftist idiocy. And the corruption comes from the top down. The Royal family is as guilty and malevolent towards their own people as the government is. 

My future and that of my family is no longer here in the UK. It’s hardest on my wife and kids because they’re British. They were born here. My wife can trace her British heritage to many centuries back. Almost a millennium. This is her home. And even she no longer wants any part of it. 

I wish I could fight this fight for all the truly amazing people of Britain. And there are many. But they won’t fight for themselves, and I’m just one person who has now lost all respect for this place. 

I never gave up on Britain. Britain gave up on Britain. And my kids deserve far better. I wish there was another way, another way for my wife to stay and be proud to be British. But that’s dead now.

text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, Kansas State and NFL receiver Kevin Lockett, born on this day in 1974 in Tulsa.

Lockett earned All-State honors as a senior at Booker T. Washington in 1991, completing his high school career with 115 receptions for 1,052 yards.

He was also a standout basketball player for the Hornets, earning special recognition All-State honors from the Tulsa World.

Lockett picked Kansas State over several other offers and in Manhattan, Lockett was a two-time first-team all conference and two-time second-team all conference performer. He also earned third team All-American as a senior in 1996.

When he completed his collegiate career, Lockett was the Wildcats' all-time leader in receptions (217), receiving yards (3,032) and receiving touchdowns (26).

Lockett was selected by the Kansas City Chiefs in the second round of the 1997 NFL Draft. In a seven-year NFL career, Lockett played for the Chiefs, Washington Redskins, Jacksonville Jaguars and New York Jets, completing his pro career with 130 catches, 1,738 yards and eight touchdowns.

He also has the distinction of having completed both of his pass attempts for touchdowns.

In 2020, Lockett was inducted into the Booker T. Washington Ring of Honor and in 2024 the K-State Athletics Hall of Fame.

While all three of Lockett's career receiving records have since been broken, I'm sure he won't mind -- since they were broken by his son, Tyler, who attended K-State between 2011 and 2014.

Happy birthday Kevin! #tdfn #okpreps @BookerTFootball @KStateFB

text:
Arlington’s Confederate memorial is back in the news over the words on a sign.

The Washington Post reported that Trump administration officials have replaced the interpretive sign at the site of the former Confederate Memorial in Arlington National Cemetery. The new version drops language that said the 32-foot bronze statue “mythologized” the Confederacy and offered “sanitized” depictions of slavery.

What’s left on the ground is the granite base. The bronze sculpture by Confederate veteran Moses Ezekiel was taken down in December 2023 after a congressionally created Naming Commission called it problematic from top to bottom. The commission and cemetery materials pointed to Lost Cause imagery: a “mammy” figure, an enslaved man following his owner to war, and a Latin inscription that framed the Confederacy as a noble lost cause.

In 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the statue would be refurbished and returned to Section 16 near Ezekiel’s grave, calling the earlier removal the work of “woke lemmings” and saying the administration honors history rather than erasing it. Restoration is expected around 2027 and has been estimated at about $10 million. The Army has said it will add new interpretive content when the sculpture comes back.

So the fight is no longer only about whether the monument stands. It is about what visitors are told it meant.

One side sees the old sign as overdue honesty about a monument that romanticized a slaveholding rebellion on the nation’s most sacred military ground. The other sees official criticism of the memorial as present-day politics written onto the past, and wants a more traditional “reconciliation” framing.

The statue is still in storage. The base is still there. The wording on the sign just changed. That small plaque is now another front in the larger argument over how the Civil War is described on federal land.

Taking the editorial adjectives off the plaque seems to me to be a modest, defensible move!

text:
When a Blackout Brings Hope: Why Turkmen Soldiers Want to Leave the Army — and the Country

Sometimes a single small detail reveals far more about the state of a country than dozens of official statements about “stability and prosperity.”

According to https://t.co/E04pJHGd5j, at least three cases have become known over the past month in which former members of Turkmenistan’s Armed Forces were prevented from leaving the country. The outlet suggests that this may indicate a broader travel ban imposed on former military personnel.

The reasons why they want to leave are equally telling.

Military personnel are reportedly dissatisfied with low incomes, inadequate social benefits, embezzlement, and deteriorating morale within the armed forces. According to the report, the situation worsened further after the authorities ended the practice of transferring service housing into military personnel’s private ownership. Many now prefer to leave the military and seek work abroad: several months of employment in Belarus, Russia, or Poland can allow them to support their families far more effectively.

And what solution is offered in response?

Improve service conditions? Raise salaries? Investigate embezzlement? Carry out reforms?

No. The more familiar solution appears to be much simpler — do not let them leave.

Another episode reported in the article is particularly revealing. During the blackout on 30 August, personnel in some military units reportedly believed that a coup d’état was beginning.

And the most striking detail is this: the soldiers reportedly felt hopeful.

But electricity was restored within several hours. According to the report, the blackout had been caused by an accident at the Mary State Power Plant. The soldiers’ hopes were not fulfilled.

At this point, there is little room left for sarcasm. If people entrusted with defending the state perceive the possibility of a coup not with fear, but with hope, the authorities should perhaps be asking not how to close the border to them, but why such sentiments exist in the first place.

Yet Turkmenistan once again appears to be choosing a familiar formula: restrictions instead of reforms, prohibitions instead of addressing the causes of discontent, and “no-exit” status instead of the freedom to leave.

People can be kept inside a country by closing the border.

But no border can force them to believe in the state.

Source: https://t.co/E04pJHGd5j, 4 September 2026

text:
Unfortunately, the city is no longer dealing just with the usual water challenges of the past century ...

The Absurd, Unending Quest to Floodproof the New York City Subway
NYT Gift Article
Listen · 28:09 min
By Mark Chiusano
08SEP2026, 
https://t.co/u2MsmxTWrp
In an era of heavy rain, a transit system with 47,000 openings is bound to leak.

... The rain has become worse — a lot worse.

That’s a function of New York’s changing climate, now considered a humid subtropical zone. 

Hotter air brings bigger and quicker deluges — known as cloudbursts — which more regularly overwhelm the sewers and turn into floods. 

New Yorkers know that this isn’t the rain of their youth, and the numbers bear it out. In the past year alone, the city has experienced multiple summer flooding events bigger than any New York had seen since 2021. 

So far in 2026, the city’s flash-flood emergency plan has been activated more than a quarter of the time. Louise Yeung, the city’s chief climate officer, calls torrential rain our “new climate reality.”

It’s the subway that suffers. In the last 20 years, at least 200 of the system’s 472 stations have been “impacted by one or more of these torrential rainfall events,” according to the M.T.A.’s climate resilience road map. 

New Yorkers have filmed so many viral videos of water rushing down stairs or next to subway doors that they’ve become a recognizable social media genre. 

There will only be more; already this year, clips circulated of a soaked subway car, a tree impaling a northbound 4 train, and a woman being swept away while trying to lunge off a bus.

Rain is a sneaky kind of climate threat: regular, low-grade, sloshing discomfort at your shins that becomes hazardous if allowed to rise. 

When it rains in New York, water is supposed to flow into the sewers, via openings along the curb, and through 7,500 miles of pipes out into processing plants or the sea. 

But many of the pipes can handle only around 1.5 inches of rain an hour; more than that, and water accumulates on the street and searches for a different way down. 

The subway obliges — it has more than 47,000 openings.

At 116th Street, I went aboveground to meet Jamie Torres-Springer, the M.T.A.’s president of construction and development, and Eric Wilson, senior vice president for climate and land use planning within the M.T.A.’s construction and development team. 

The intersection was busy with delivery bikers, fast food spots and people trying to sell something — the kind of activity that tends to scatter during a storm. 

Torres-Springer and Wilson brought me to the southwestern corner entrance to observe the most obvious opening to the underground: the stairs, which the city has been trying to rainproof. 

There, commuters going down to catch the train now first step up onto what is essentially a concrete platform, and then descend. 

This small elevation is a surprisingly crucial seven-inch barrier that can stop water from surging down the stairs.

Another kind of opening is offered by the subway’s many air vents, used instead of air-conditioning — also a consequence of 19th-century engineering. 

Shallow pans sit a few feet below the vents to catch and drain water while still letting air in — at 116th Street, I saw a rat scamper through the gap. 

Today, those pans are regularly inundated, and the M.T.A. sometimes makes do by covering the vents with grimy yellow mats. 

Torres-Springer humbly called them a “low-tech solution.”

The transit system’s 2025-29 capital plan allocated $223 million for light-touch subway protections like these. 

And at 116th Street, they seem to be helping: After $1.4 million of work, a spokeswoman said the M.T.A. hadn’t seen flooding at the station since they were implemented. 

Elevated steps or vents have been added to a few dozen others, with similar mitigations planned for an additional 100.

But these tweaks are small, and if they fail, the results could be grim. 

Transit experts who think about subway flooding often reference the 2021 Zhengzhou metro disaster, in which water trapped people in train cars and rose up to their chests. 

Multiple people drowned. 

New York City’s transit system has so far escaped that nightmare scenario, but there are always opportunities for mayhem and injuries, given that six inches of moving water can knock riders off their feet. 

The subway is full of sharp edges and freakish accidents on good days. It is creaky and old like Paris’s and London’s, systems that are also water-vulnerable — and even those don’t have New York’s “confluence of risks,” as Wilson pointed out. 

“We’re a coastal city,” he said, and “we’re a riverine city.”

Five years after Ida, the M.T.A. has not yet made protective changes to more than half of the system’s flood-prone stations. 

All the while, the rain continues to fall.

New York City has been preoccupied with the destructive potential of water for years, but the fear was water from the sea rather than the sky. 

Every subway worker, after all, has a story from Hurricane Sandy, which forced thousands to evacuate, shuttered the stock exchange and, overall, did $19 billion worth of damage in 2012. 

It was “the big one,” in the words of James Rudolph, a retired transit cop. 

With power entirely down for days across Lower Manhattan, transit officers got air down to their underground headquarters at Canal Street by leaving the door open. 

“The rats were having a field day,” Rudolph says. “They were running in and running out.”

Karen Grigoryan, now the subway’s superintendent for hydraulics, spent days after the storm trying to avoid breathing diesel fumes while struggling to pump seawater out of various subway tubes. 

He operated a special train with portable pumps and hoses to funnel the water up and out of the tunnel. 

And it was all hands on deck; he couldn’t leave. 

“I had to stay at work around the clock and pump the water,” he remembers. 

He was still stuck underground when his son was born en route to the hospital in an ambulance.

Biju Varughese normally did train repair work underneath cars in the enormous 207th Street yard, home to an overhaul shop and a resting place for off-duty A and C trains. 

That day, though, the space where he and some 550 people usually worked was completely flooded. 

Varughese showed up, but he could see only with a flashlight. 

Outside, the whole 62-track yard was a waterway, too, an extension of the Harlem River that had overwhelmed a bare-bones fence. 

“It was like hell,” he said.

The devastation of Sandy initiated a colossal building and rebuilding spree in New York. 

Engineers mapped out mammoth coastal defense projects, some of which are still in progress, like a 19-foot-high Staten Island sea wall. 

Others are fully or partly in place, like the long portions of the Lower Manhattan coast being raised or protected by the East Side Coastal Resiliency project.

And little expense was spared: Senator Chuck Schumer’s office called the influx the “largest federal revitalization of New York infrastructure since Robert Moses.” 

The M.T.A. alone got more than $6 billion, which covered big coastal projects, rehabilitated tunnels and helped protect stations and infrastructure from storm surge, taking years to spend down. 

(Sandy’s damage was also measurably severe, leading Congress to pass a stand-alone relief bill.)

Nine years later, though, before a lot of this construction was finished, Ida reached the southern edge of New York City. 

It was merely a post-tropical cyclone by then, but it made a mess of the rush-hour commute. On the streets, the pavement seemed to disappear. 

Rosa Almonte was driving a city bus on Queens Boulevard at the end of a 10-hour shift when she realized that water had risen up to the seats; her passengers tried to find places to perch above it. 

Almonte felt the bus moving, and not by her wheel.

But the bigger problems were below ground. 

Water flowed into basement apartments, where 11 people died. 

And it cascaded easily into the subway. 

Rushing water shot down station steps, white horses stampeding to catch an uptown express. It was a sight that would, many times, be likened to Niagara Falls, including by Bryan Roman, a 1 train operator, who approached the rapids along flooded tracks. 

“It looked like something exploded,” he told The City Reporter.

The two storms — and the ways to protect against them — were very different. 

Sandy’s vengeance from below was brutal, 14-foot surges of waves and corroding salt, but the weak points were obvious, and concentrated along the coast. 

Even though Ida wasn’t as financially destructive, it highlighted a host of new danger zones across the city, because rain can fall inland as easily as waterside. 

All the post-Sandy work to fortify against surge along New York’s 520 miles of coast wasn’t much help. 

Congress sent less money to the M.T.A. for recovery — a lot less, on the order of tens of millions instead of billions. 

That meant that the agency was harder pressed for cash to protect itself from the new threat, one that appears to be hitting more often than Sandy-style hurricanes. 

The current and future weather reality is Ida — again and again.

text:
The Absurd, Unending Quest to Floodproof the New York City Subway

NYT Gift Article
Listen · 28:09 min
By Mark Chiusano
08SEP2026, 
https://t.co/vHcU510Ekr
In an era of heavy rain, a transit system with 47,000 openings is bound to leak.

Mark Chiusano made repeat visits to five stations and spoke with more than 20 experts over the course of two months to report this article.

On a baking hot day in July, I took the 2 train to the 116th Street station at Malcolm X Boulevard in Harlem. 

The station’s name shone from the wall on ocean-blue tile, along with glass mosaics of jazz musicians and civil rights leaders. 

The place looked, unsurprisingly, a little worn; paint was flaking around a gash in the subceiling and off some of the green platform columns, and the Langston Hughes mosaic panel was stained brown from dripping water. 

Water also glimmered in the tracks, mixed with trash.

I was there to meet some of the top construction executives for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the entity that runs the subways, to see what it would take to floodproof the system.

The 116th Street station was shipwrecked during Hurricane Ida in 2021, which dumped a record-breaking 7 to 9 inches of rain across the city — a total liquid weight of some 160 million tons. 

Sheets of water from the ceiling cascaded onto one of the platforms — engulfing the green columns, obscuring some of that mosaic tile and drowning the tracks below. 

If the water hadn’t been dirty and underground, it might have looked like a water park attraction, the trains like logs speeding through a flume. 

The water came down from air vents cut into the sidewalk, which became funnels when enough water gathered on the surface.

The station is among the oldest and most flood-prone in the city. 

The area’s former state senator — and later New York governor — David Paterson remembers it being a problem zone as far back as the late 1970s. 

“If you wanted to start working out, and you wanted to maybe do some swimming, all you had to do was go to 116th Street-Lenox Avenue,” Paterson told me. 

“By the time you got to the bottom of the stairs, you’d be immersed in water.”

The conditions of the station’s construction explain why subway flooding is so hard to stop. 

More than 120 years ago, the first portions of the transit system were built mostly by hand. 

The Manhattan schist bedrock was hard and expensive to cut through, so stations like 116th Street were formed in shallow trenches — meaning that rain never had to travel very deep to cause chaos. 

Water periodically seeped up from below too, as tunnel workers uncovered ancient underground streams while excavating; since then, holes have been periodically plugged and patched with concrete and grout. 

Again and again, the M.T.A. has been forced to jury-rig solutions.

Even as construction technology advanced over the years, these problems persisted. 

The subway was largely locally funded for decades, predating the strong 20th-century federal government that opened its checkbook for more-modern mass transit in Washington and San Francisco. 

Cue eternal financial issues, which breed political and operational ones. Underground, there is always something else to fix.

text:
🚨 Kevin O'Leary's $11 Million Baseball Card, Live on CNBC ⚾💰

"Mr. Wonderful" brought some serious hardware to Squawk Box this week — literally chaining himself to an $11 million baseball card on live TV. The card: Shohei Ohtani's 1-of-1 Back to Back Gold Logoman Autograph Relic, part of Topps Chrome's 2026 set honoring the three players who won major 2024-2025 awards (Ohtani, Aaron Judge, and Tarik Skubal).

The backstory is almost as wild as the price tag. An anonymous collector at a small hobby shop in Boca Raton, Florida pulled the card from a Topps Chrome pack in late July. Collector Matthew "Shyne" Allen had already put out a $6.5 million public bounty on Instagram before the card even surfaced — but once it did, a Hong Kong trading card firm offered $10 million, forcing Allen and his partners to move fast. He ultimately paid over $10 million, with the final transaction landing at $11 million.

The buyer: Secure Collectibles, an investment group co-founded by Kevin O'Leary alongside Allen and entrepreneur Paul Warshaw. This isn't their first record-breaking grab either — the same trio previously paid nearly $13 million for a dual-signed Michael Jordan/Kobe Bryant card, which still holds the all-time record. Ohtani's card now ranks as the third-highest public sports card sale ever, trailing only that Jordan/Kobe card and a 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle that sold for $12.6 million.

Whether you see this as smart alternative-asset diversification or pure spectacle, the trend is real: high-net-worth collectors are increasingly treating rare sports memorabilia like a genuine asset class — complete with bounties, syndicates, and 3 a.m. Zoom calls to close deals, as O'Leary described his Jordan/Kobe purchase.

Wild watches, wild cards — collectibles investing is having a moment.

text:
🚨Duty Chronicles #1: About Me and The Truth About Why I Was Raided by State Narcotics Agents back in 2020

"It's peak Southern hypocrite culture when attempted murderers, wife-beaters, adulterers, embezzlers, and alcoholics look down their noses at medical cannabis patients — then pray for them on Sunday mornings because they're 'potheads' and 'sinners' in need of forgiveness."  ---- Me

My name is Scott Enlow.

I graduated from our state fire academy and our 
capital city’s police academy, completed training at 
the National Fire Academy in Emmitsburg, Maryland, 
and attended United States Marshals Service 
Academy training at the Federal Law Enforcement 
Training Center (FLETC) in Glynco, Georgia. I was 
designated a U.S. Customs officer and served as a 
member of the now-defunct U.S. Customs Blue 
Lightning Drug Interdiction Strike Force in the mid-
1990s and early 2000s, and I completed more 
than 2,200 hours of additional fire and police training.

The fire service and law enforcement was my career and it was my passion in life.

I began my fire career at age 18 and served twenty-seven years. I served as a municipal firefighter, fire officer and arson investigator. 

Concurrently, I held the elected office of county constable for twelve years, a role in my state where constables, as sworn law enforcement officers, aid the sheriff through general county law enforcement and civil process service for district Justice Courts.     

I suppose one encounter during my tenure as constable encapsulated an undeserved (I believe) reputation: while serving a court summons, I introduced myself to the recipient. 

He shook my hand and proudly declared, “Oh, you’re Scott Enlow? I’ve heard of you—you’re an asshole. I like that. I voted for you.” 

I thanked him, recognizing the compliment beneath his blunt words. I knew what he meant.      

Since 2010, I have been retired from public service, finding solace in the quiet joys of family life. 

My firefighting career and its 24 hours on/off x3 then four days off schedule gave us four days off at a time. So like many in the profession, I supplemented my income with diverse side ventures. 

Before my election as constable, I worked as a home inspector for an insurance company, a security guard, a private investigator, a store clerk, a fire equipment salesman, a process server, and a city animal control officer. I also owned a chimney sweep service business. 

A part-time town policeman and part-time deputy sheriff. 

From age sixteen to thirty-two, I volunteered as a firefighter in my community on several departments, serving as a volunteer fire chief from 1992 to 1996. 

During that same period, I served as the county’s unpaid arson investigator, a sheriff-appointed role I took on to gain law enforcement experience and county-funded training, paving the way for my future political run as constable.    

In retirement, my passions tether me to family, history and the natural world. I collect antique lamps, vintage fishing lures, fire memorabilia, and relics of local history. 

With permission, I search for Native American arrowheads on private lands. I grow Koi in my pond and feed wildlife and birds.  

My patio flower garden flourishes, and I find an unfamiliar peace in watching them slowly grow into something beautiful.

Though once an avid hunter, I no longer hunt, having lost all taste for it. Nowadays I simply don't like the killing of defenseless animals. I catch bugs and put them outside rather than killing them. The funds I once spent on hunting leases and outdoor adventures I now spend to feed wildlife in winter and rescue stray animals that are abandoned.       

I once crafted handmade knives from obsidian and flint through the ancient art of flint knapping, a craft I loved until chronic elbow pain forced me to set it aside.      

My story, however, is not without its trials.       

In 1985, during training at the state fire academy, I dislocated/broke my elbow. After the bone healed and much exercising, I was able to return to duty — any major effects from the injury lay dormant until 2001, when moderate and sometimes severe chronic pain emerged.       

Orthopedic specialists diagnosed severe osteoarthritis, bone-on-bone friction, and three bone fragments adrift in scar tissue around the joint.

 Surgery was deemed risky: one doctor warned it could worsen the scar tissue, while another offered to remove the fragments but could not promise pain relief. Both agreed a total elbow replacement was not an option.       

Their recommendation? Anti-inflammatories, ice, and try not to think about it.     

The pain soon compromised my ability to perform essential firefighting tasks, particularly lifting the heavy Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools overhead, a large part of my job at the time. My left arm, besieged by pain, sometimes faltered under such demands.       

I turned to cortisone and anesthetic injections directly into the elbow, heralded as effective for osteoarthritis. Yet the procedure itself was agonizing—worse than the chronic pain itself. The needle’s intrusion, the subsequent swelling, and, on one occasion, blood dripping from the injection site left me in torment. The fleeting relief was not worth the ordeal, and I abandoned the injections.       

After nerve conduction tests, physical therapy, and trials of non-narcotic medications proved ineffective, my doctor enrolled me in a pain management program.

I signed a contract, agreeing to seek treatment solely from this provider, submit to regular drug tests, and acknowledge the risk of addiction. 

At the time, I failed to grasp the full implications of the term “addiction.” The emphasis was on preventing recreational abuse, not the inevitable physical dependency of long-term use.    

From November 2001 to January 2020, my schedule revolved around monthly doctor visits, usually accompanied by mandatory urinalysis, followed by a thirty-day hydrocodone prescription. 

Though imperfect, this regimen allowed me to continue to work and live actively without constant pain.   

Everything continued like clockwork until after I retired from the fire department at the end of 2010.  

Over time, the pills’ effectiveness waned. Increasing the dosage was the only path to sustained relief—an option neither I nor my doctor fully supported.

Instead, citing the “opioid epidemic” and tightened prescribing guidelines, my doctor actually reduced my monthly prescription by 25%. I made it work, and the pain management monthly appointments continued.

But at some point, after lengthy reflection, I recognized that I was sliding down a slippery slope greased with hydrocodone.    

I relied on them too much while I was serving as my mother’s hospice caretaker until her death in 2015.

Then again in 2019, while serving as my father’s hospice caretaker until his passing. I admit, during those times the pills blunted my emotions and made things not hurt so bad. That's all I'll say about that. Worst times of my life.       

After daddy died, I experienced a profound shift in life perspective. Determined to reclaim my physical and mental health, I resolved to abandon pain pills that I knew were harming me, turning to over-the-counter analgesics, heat and cold therapy, and even considering acupuncture.       

I also discovered the miracle of CBD and sometimes ate gummies containing the anti-inflammatory cannabinoid.       

On January 4, 2020, at a doctor’s appointment, I declared my intent to quit hydrocodone. My doctor cautioned against abrupt cessation and offered a reduced 30 day prescription of 75 instead of 90 to taper off. 

When he stepped out, I told the nurse I would not take it, left the script behind, and walked out.      

I had vowed to stop at the year’s start, and the moment had arrived. My resolve was firm, but the consequences would test me.     

For nineteen long years, I had taken (at least) three (3) 10mg Hydrocodone pills daily—one at waking, one after lunch, one at bedtime—totaling roughly 20,520 pills. Then........I stopped cold turkey.       

It was a reckless choice, driven by a need for a clean break. The doctor had predicted a week to ten days of “uncomfortable” flu-like symptoms should I decide to stop abruptly. But the reality was far graver.  Maybe partly because of my mid-50's age.   

Three days after my last dose, severe withdrawal-like symptoms set in, and they gripped me for over six weeks. Night sweats drenched my sheets and pillow. I lost my appetite, endured muscle weakness, migraines, chills, diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration. 

My chronic elbow and shoulder pain resurfaced, joined by new aches. I shed over twenty pounds, and my mental health teetered on the brink.      

Temptation beckoned—a partial prescription remained in my wife’s safe—but with her help, I held firm. I knew Suboxone was an option to treat withdrawals, but I wanted nothing more to do with pills or strips or anything opioid-related. 

I told myself I'd tough it out.

A trip to a detox facility was an option, but in our small county, I feared gossip. So I chose to endure alone, a decision I now see as unwise but deeply personal.

Seeking relief online, I read about cannabis aiding opioid cessation. I saw hope when a California-based tele-medicine provider described medical cannabis’s success in West Coast recovery clinics.   

Knowing medical cannabis was already legal in 33 states at the time felt terribly unfair to me. So sitting on the toilet one morning at 2am with cold sweat draining down my face and back I finally said, "screw that". 

Desperate and willing to risk legal consequences, I made the conscious decision to disregard the law and began ordering small quantities, a few grams at a time, of “live resin” through the mail.

It wasn't difficult to find a mail order supplier online. Many vendors exist that ship illegal cannabis and/or legal hemp flower, edibles and concentrates through the mail.    

The sticky, pungent-smelling plant resin called live resin is rich in anti-inflammatory cannabinoids, but it also has a higher-than-legal THC content.      

I carefully mixed one gram of resin with 30ml (2 tablespoons) of heated olive oil. That made 30 doses. I took a 1cc dose sublingually twice daily, delivering approximately 10 milligrams of THC and 15 milligrams of CBD. A moderate but effective dose.       

The relief was swift, easing both withdrawals and the constant elbow, shoulder, and back pain. My appetite returned. Food tasted good again. I wanted to eat again. 

Though not a panacea, it made my pain manageable with Tylenol and ibuprofen.      

I naively assumed my modest shipments —insignificant compared to the fentanyl flooding the nation—would go unnoticed. I was very mistaken.

After several months and three orders, a postal inspector flagged my little incoming package, alerting state narcotics police. 

One morning, seven bureau of narcotics agents in tactical gear, armed with automatic patrol rifles, ambushed me as I retrieved my mail.       

Concealed in my neighbor’s driveway, bushes, and a nearby logging road, they converged as I walked back to my house in pajamas and house slippers, holding a small Priority Mail box that felt empty.    

The seized package contained ~ten grams of cannabis resin—a piece about as big as an olive equivalent to two nickels in weight—and a single purple-colored cannabis cigarette the seller had thrown in the package as a freebie. 

A total value of $250 in California. That's what I'd paid, using my credit card.       

A thorough search of my home yielded nothing illegal. And the search was very thorough, believe me.      

The agents confiscated my computer, my wife’s computer, her employer’s computer she worked on at home, and my cellphone for forensic analysis, allegedly suspecting evidence of drug transactions.

They were also looking for anything unrelated and illegal that they could find. But there was nothing there for them to find. 

They found absolutely nothing illegal, and all of the devices were returned a year later via my attorney.       

The agents departed my home that day without arresting me, a leniency my lawyer attributed to COVID-19 protocols at the time.    

They instructed me to have my lawyer contact the district attorney’s office, then drove off in their unmarked pickup trucks, leaving me standing on my front porch, my arm hurting, with no medicine.

Gossip spread swiftly after a passerby witnessed the armed and camouflaged agents and called a former coworker of mine, sparking rumors of an FBI raid. 

The former coworker called to alert another former coworker I had been raided, and before you know it, the whole county knew SOMETHING happened, though no one knew exactly what. 

Naturally, the very worst was assumed because computers were seized. 

That single phone call started a very ugly gossip mill to start turning.      

Thirty days later I was charged with a felony for possessing more than two grams but less than ten grams of THC.       

A year later, I pleaded guilty in circuit court before a  judge. The assistant district attorney asked for a ten-year prison sentence and a $5,000 fine, but the judge imposed a $3,500 fine and four years of probation instead.      

After I paid the fine in full days later, the judge dismissed the charges and terminated my probation after only sixty days, non-adjudicating the case. 

It was over. 

The ordeal was lifted, releasing a crushing psychological weight.       

Less than a year later, my state legalized medical marijuana. I was among the first to secure a doctor’s recommendation and a medical card.      

The option to use cannabis transformed my life; this plant liberated me from dangerous pain-killing narcotic pills, monthly doctor visits, and costly prescriptions. I was also able to stop taking a nightly controlled-substance sleeping pill and a daily anti-anxiety medication.       

My physical and mental health have flourished from having the option to self-medicate with a natural medicine, only as needed, instead of taking dangerous pills on an 8-hour schedule forever.          

Today, I live freely and in robust health, cherishing days spent with my young grandson. My quality of life is vibrant, serene and profoundly fulfilling, and I would not change a moment of it.    

Regrettably, I lost some friends amid all of this. One loss surprised me more than most: a close friend—almost a brother—of more than thirty years turned his back on me and now treats me like a stranger. 

Last year, my wife and I ran into him in an aisle at Lowe’s. We called his name, genuinely happy to see him, but he brushed past us while staring straight ahead, like we were a bad smell—as though I had committed an unforgivable or unspeakable crime. 

We were shocked.   

Later, I thought: I suppose if my choices disappoint you so deeply, then I sincerely apologize for that disappointment. Please go on and enjoy your life.   Because in the end, I do what I believe is best for me, not what others deem acceptable.     

---- A. Scott Enlow
