text:
Harvard Law offers students fidget toys, ‘low sensory rooms’ | Matt Lamb, The College Fix

OPINION: Safe spaces and coloring rooms are still with us

As that nation’s future Supreme Court justices, solicitors general, and elite law firm attorneys start school at Harvard University, the Ivy League is ensuring they have everything they need to take a “break from the noise.”

The freshman orientation for new Harvard law students reportedly promoted “low sensory rooms,” according to National Review.

The rooms include “weighted blankets, dim lighting, fidget toys, and more,” according to reporter Abigail Anthony.

Anthony opined: “Of course, the people being trained to work 80 hours a week at a Big Law Firm cannot be expected to manage a couple hours of orientation events without palliative care.”

Students can also relax in wellness lounges with “massage chairs” and “lowkey crafts and activities.”

The school reportedly informed students of the dozens of “gender-inclusive bathrooms” on campus as well.

Reactions to the news were mixed.

One person commented on the National Review article and said, “This is overkill, but providing a quiet space for those who experience sensory overload is both reasonable and humane.”

Another wrote: “If someone handed me a fidget toy or a colouring book with which to relax at work, I’d just be embarrassed.”

The fidget toys and childlike activities are nothing new – in fact colleges rolled them out during the “safe space” era of the mid-2010s and then subsequently to help students cope with Donald Trump’s presidential election in 2016 and 2024.

The Fix previously reported on the 2016 response:

The University of Pennsylvania created a “breathing space” for students troubled by the Trump win, complete with coloring books and craft-making, along with a puppy and some cats to cuddle.

Students at Cornell University held a “cry-in” regarding the outcome, with one student saying she was “quite terrified, honestly.”

Activists at fellow Ivies Yale, Brown, and Harvard had demanded their universities become “sanctuary” campuses for undocumented students because Trump had threatened to end the DACA, the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, program.

The University of Michigan Law School held a post-election event featuring “self-care activities such as coloring sheets, play dough, [and] positive card-making.”

If Harvard Law needs a few more toys, I still have a stuffed dinosaur from my own “safe space.”

In 1st part of 2-part conversation, @NotreDame’s @PatrickDeneen talks to @GivingReview’s @mhartmannmke about his new book American Odyssey, the innate American tension between rootedness and restlessness, perfectibility and progressivism, utopianism, and how all these impulses have shaped grantmaking, as well as what “Moonlight” Graham in Field of Dreams might teach us about localism and the meaning of philanthropy.

“We are more homeless at the moment than we are at home,” according to Deneen—literally, for younger Americans struggling to settle, buy homes, and start families, but also because technology leaves us elsewhere even when at home. Americans remain as “anxious and restless as Tocqueville described us in the 19th Century.”

That restlessness, Deneen says, feeds a belief in perfectibility—the sense that “there’s something beyond, outside, something around the corner that might be better.” The Progressive Era may have represented a “full realization” and “institutionalization” of those impulses, including in philanthropy.

He contrasts an older, face-to-face charity, rooted in particular places, with modern philanthropy’s organized pursuit of transformation and progress.

And he offers Graham as unlikely exemplar of local rootedness. The story of Graham, whose one-inning major-league baseball career gave way to decades serving as a small-town Minnesota doctor and community pillar, raises a different possibility for philanthropy—staying somewhere alongside and serving the people there.

text:
CARLINA WHITE — THE WOMAN WHO DISCOVERED SHE HAD BEEN ABDUCTED

Carlina Renae White was born on 15 July 1987. Nineteen days later, on 4 August 1987, her parents, Joy White and Carl Tyson, took her to Harlem Hospital in New York because she had a fever of about 104 degrees. A woman dressed as a nurse comforted the frightened teenage mother and moved through the ward as if she belonged there. In the early morning hours someone removed the infant’s intravenous line and carried her out. Hospital cameras were not working. A reward was offered. The case went cold.
Carlina grew up as Nejdra “Netty” Nance, principally in Bridgeport, Connecticut, raised by Annugetta “Ann” Pettway. As she got older she noticed gaps. Pettway could not produce a proper birth certificate when Carlina needed identification. The physical resemblance between supposed mother and daughter was poor. Carlina eventually searched missing-child databases, saw infant photographs from the 1987 Harlem case, and recognized her own face. She contacted the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children. Police took DNA from Carlina and from Joy White and Carl Tyson. In January 2011 the match was confirmed.
The reunion after approximately 23 years was joyful and disorienting. Carlina said it felt like being born again. Pettway was later charged and pleaded guilty to kidnapping. She received a 12-year sentence and was released after serving about nine years and eight months. Carlina’s case is unusual because the missing child became the investigator. The hospital, the police, and the passage of time had failed. The adult survivor assembled the evidence of her own abduction.

Country: United States

text:
Tall Whites, Eisenhower, and Area 51

The story that “Tall Whites” lived at Area 51 and that President Dwight D. Eisenhower secretly met Nordic aliens in 1954 is UFO legend rather than documented history. Area 51, associated with Groom Lake, became a highly classified aerospace testing site. The CIA and Air Force used it for aircraft programs including the U-2, A-12 OXCART, and F-117. Its secrecy and high-altitude flights contributed to numerous Cold War UFO reports. The government publicly acknowledged the facility in 2013.

On February 20, 1954, Eisenhower was staying at Smoke Tree Ranch in Palm Springs. According to the official explanation, he left after dinner for emergency dental treatment after damaging a crown. Rumors of his death followed his absence. Researchers at the Eisenhower Presidential Library found no evidence that he secretly traveled to Edwards Air Force Base. Later UFO accounts transformed the incident into a supposed meeting with tall, pale, white-haired extraterrestrials called Nordics or Tall Whites. They allegedly offered advanced technology in exchange for nuclear disarmament, but no reliable records, photographs, or witnesses confirm the meeting. An early source was a 1954 letter attributed to Gerald Light.

The Area 51 Tall White legend largely comes from Charles Hall, a weather observer stationed at Indian Springs from 1965 to 1967. In Millennial Hospitality, Hall described tall, pale humanoids living underground, operating advanced spacecraft, and visiting Las Vegas with government escorts. Hall initially presented his account as fiction before later treating it as factual.

Despite decades of speculation, no physical evidence, documents, photographs, or independent witnesses have established Tall Whites. Official investigations have found no verified evidence of extraterrestrial spacecraft or beings. Area 51’s documented history remains secret aerospace testing, while the extraterrestrial stories persist.

text:
The first primary school I went to was a C of E (Church of England) school. C of E schools are state funded, secular, and free to attend. Despite being secular, they are open to children of any background including religion, and are meant to retain a Christian characteristic. The one I attended certainly had a Christian characteristic. It was called Christ Church School, and was in St Leonards-on-Sea, Hastings. It had a large gothic church (which is still there) called Christ Church next to it. Assemblies were held in the church, where hymns were sung, and the Lord's Prayer was recited. The school itself moved to newly built premises fairly nearby, after either my first or second year at the school. My brother, who's around two years my senior, wanted to move schools, so I moved with him to the final primary school I attended, which was West St Leonards School in Hastings. This school was likely a C of E school as well, as there were morning assemblies in which hymns were sung, and although I have no clear recollection, the Lord's Prayer was likely recited on occasion. This school had a large recreational field attached to it, and two fairly large playgrounds. The secondary school (which in the US and other places is called a high school) I attended was a state school (which is free to attend and open to those within the catchment area). Fee paying private schools in the UK are also referred to as public schools, the linguistic reasoning behind this was because they were open to children from any locality. In the US, Canada, Australia and other places, a public school refers to a free to attend state funded school. The secondary school I went to was called the Grove School, and was for all intents and purposes a fairly rough school. 
Neither of my parents are religious, but are spiritual sentient beings nonetheless. This is as true today as it was then.
As a child and as an adult, I would visit my maternal grandparents in Hove, East Sussex. Hove was then a town, but is now part of Brighton & Hove City. I have fond memories of my grandmother, especially of when visiting her as a child. I remember my grandfather as being a fairly grumpy distant man, but as someone who was ultimately able to provide for his family. They ran a successful business together, which I think mostly involved sourcing furniture for restaurants in the Brighton & Hove area. Their names were Jack and Norma Waring. Norma died aged 90 in 2016, and to the best of my recollection, Jack died around ten years earlier at the age of 88. I don't think they would have described themselves as religious, but from time to time, both Jack and Norma attended Brighton & Hove Reform Synagogue, and later Brighton & Hove Progressive Synagogue. Neither of them were particularly political, and their attendance at either synagogue would have been for the community value that was offered. As a pre-adolescent child I went once with my grandmother to the Reform synagogue, and it was during Hanukkah, which was something I had not heard of before. I remember there was food, some other children there, and a talk by the Rabbi that included the story attached to the festival. My pre-adolescent child self's understanding of Hanukkah after this was basically, it's a festival similar to Christmas in that gifts are given in December, some Greeks a long time ago were the bad guys in this particular story, in which there was some lamp oil that lasted longer than it should have. 
My grandparents and extended family celebrated Christmas, and with my parents and siblings, I would often spend time with them over this period.

text:
September 8, 2026

Don't Be Anxious 

By Michael A. Youssef, Ph.D.

Read Matthew 6:25-34.

At the root of all anxiety is the fear that we'll lose something valuable. But no matter how many material possessions we collect or how much money we have in the bank, these things can never bring us peace or contentment. However, when we know that God gave us everything and that it's all for His glory anyway, we will be at peace. You will be at peace. Why? Because just as God gave it to you, He will multiply it to you. He will multiply it to you so that you can keep on doing the work of God. God is looking for conduits—people through whom His gifts and blessings can flow to others.

You see, fear and faith do not mix. If we're paying attention to all that the Lord is doing in the world, it's hard to live in a state of anxiety. The opposite is true as well: It's impossible to fully trust God's character, intentions, and promises if we're living in a constant state of fear.

Jesus showed that worry reveals where we are reluctant to trust God (see v. 26). But God is infinitely trustworthy—the very definition of faithful. Because God is who He is—perfectly loving, just, and sovereign—worry is pointless.

To find peace and contentment we must lose ourselves in obedience to the Lord. Worry comes from focusing on how dangerous this world is. Contentment comes by focusing on proclaiming the goodness of God in the Gospel of Jesus Christ to the lost. Worry thinks about what we don't have or what we might lose. Contentment thinks of what we have already and is yet to come—the very presence of God in glory.

Brothers and sisters, God is good. There is peace in His presence, and He wants us to have it. Serenity fills the courts of heaven, and He wants us to have this same peace in our lives. His peace cannot be fabricated, duplicated, or falsified. His peace is above and beyond explanation. Even in the midst of life's worst storms, He freely offers His peace to all who would receive it.

Prayer: Jesus, I know worry doesn't add anything good to my life, so help me turn from fear and instead exercise faith. Fill me with Your peace. I pray in the name of Jesus. Amen.

"Can any one of you by worrying add a single hour to your life?" (Matthew 6:27).

text:
The Koodathayi Cyanide Murders in Kerala is one of the most calculated and shocking cases of familial crime in post-independence India. Over a span of 14 years (2002 to 2016), the prime accused, Jolly Joseph, eliminated six members of her own family by administering potassium cyanide to usurp ancestral property, secure control over the household, and marry a man of her choice.
Background and Double Life
 * Jolly Joseph was the daughter-in-law of the respected Ponnamattam family in Koodathayi village, Kozhikode, married to Roy Thomas.
 * She maintained an elaborate facade before the family and the entire village that she was a lecturer at the National Institute of Technology (NIT Calicut). She would dress up every morning and commute with a fake NIT identity card, whereas in reality, she only ran a local beauty parlor and tailoring business.
 * Driven by the desire to gain sole control over the family's assets and eliminate anyone suspicious of her secrets, she systematically plotted to eliminate every obstacle from her path.
Chilling Sequence of Murders (2002–2016)
Over 14 years, Jolly murdered six people using potassium cyanide:
 * 1. Annamma Thomas (Mother-in-law - 2002): The matriarch, Annamma, maintained strict control over the household's finances. Jolly poisoned her by lacing mutton soup with cyanide. The family dismissed her sudden collapse as a fatal heart attack.
 * 2. Tom Thomas (Father-in-law - 2008): When he stood in the way of transferring the family property into her and her husband's names, Jolly poisoned him through food/capsules. Following his death, Jolly produced a forged will claiming the entire estate.
 * 3. Roy Thomas (Husband - 2011): Strained by Roy's severe alcoholism and mounting financial troubles, their marriage deteriorated. Jolly served him a dinner of rice and curry laced with cyanide. An autopsy was conducted, which detected cyanide in Roy's system; however, Jolly managed to convince relatives that he had died by suicide due to unmanageable debts.
 * 4. Mathew Manchadiyil (Maternal Uncle - 2014): Annamma’s brother, Mathew, harbored deep suspicions regarding Roy’s unnatural death and the authenticity of the will. He repeatedly demanded a fresh police inquiry and post-mortem review. Jolly eliminated him by spiking his drink with cyanide.
 * 5. Alphine Shaju (Two-year-old child - 2014): Jolly had set her sights on marrying Shaju Zacharias, Roy's cousin. To remove any impediment, she murdered Shaju's two-year-old daughter, Alphine, by mixing cyanide into her food during a family communion event.
 * 6. Sily Shaju (Shaju's first wife - 2016): To clear the final path toward marrying Shaju, Jolly targeted his wife, Sily. While waiting at a dental clinic, Jolly offered Sily water and medication laced with cyanide, leading to her immediate collapse and death. In 2017, Jolly married Shaju.
Modus Operandi

TELANGANA SEEKS TO INCREASE RICE EXPORTS AND TRADE WITH THE PHILIPPINES – UTTAM

Telangana Minister for Irrigation and Food & Civil Supplies Capt. N. Uttam Kumar Reddy met Mr. Francisco P. Tu Laurel Jr., Secretary of Agriculture of the Republic of the Philippines and a member of the Philippine Cabinet, in New Delhi on Tuesday. (Mr. Francisco P. Tu Laurel Jr.’s position in Philippines is equivalent in India to that of a Union Cabinet Minister responsible for irrigation, agriculture and food.)

The two leaders held detailed discussions on the possibility of increasing rice exports and also increasing trade between Telangana and Philippines.

Uttam Kumar Reddy explained that Telangana had emerged as one of India’s leading paddy-producing states and possessed the production capacity, modern rice-milling infrastructure and experience required to supply high-quality rice in substantial quantities.

Secretary Laurel responded positively to the proposal and indicated that the Philippines would examine the possibility of sourcing larger quantities of rice from Telangana. The two sides discussed how the proposal could be taken forward through the appropriate government agencies, recognised importers, exporters and rice millers.

The discussions assume importance in view of the Philippines’ substantial requirement for imported rice and its efforts to diversify its international sources of supply. Uttam Kumar Reddy said Telangana could offer competitive prices, dependable quality and timely delivery and could emerge as a trusted long-term supplier of rice to the Philippines.

The meeting also covered rice varieties, quality standards, pricing, procurement mechanisms, logistics, certification procedures and sanitary and phytosanitary requirements. Both sides agreed that officials and industry representatives should examine these issues and prepare a practical roadmap for translating the discussions into concrete trade opportunities.

Secretary Laurel also expressed interest in procuring meat products and quality seeds from Telangana. Uttam Kumar Reddy welcomed the interest and said Telangana had strong capabilities in seed production, food processing and allied agricultural sectors. The available product categories and regulatory requirements would be examined in consultation with the relevant authorities and private-sector representatives.

Uttam Kumar said expanding agricultural exports would create new opportunities for Telangana’s farmers, rice millers, seed companies, food-processing industries and other participants in the rural economy.

“Our objective is to create dependable and remunerative international markets for Telangana’s farmers and agricultural industries. Telangana has the production capacity, processing infrastructure and entrepreneurial strength to become a reliable long-term supplier of rice and other agricultural products to the Philippines,” he said.

The leaders also discussed a wide range of issues relating to India–Philippines relations, food security, agricultural cooperation and the broader potential for increasing direct trade between Telangana and the Philippines. They observed that agriculture and food trade could become an important component of the growing strategic partnership between India and the Philippines.

Uttam Kumar Reddy and Secretary Laurel extended invitations to each other to visit their respective regions. Uttam Kumar Reddy specially invited Secretary Laurel to visit Hyderabad and participate in the Telangana Rising Summit scheduled to be held in December 2026.

The meeting concluded on a highly positive note, with both sides expressing their commitment to pursue the issues discussed and strengthen cooperation in agriculture, rice and food trade, seed development and related sectors. Uttam  said the Telangana government would coordinate with the Government of India, the Embassy of the Philippines, relevant Philippine agencies and private-sector representatives to take the proposals forward.

NCHUANWU (SCENT LEAF): THE AROMATIC LEAF BEHIND THE FLAVOUR

Have you ever opened a pot of Nigerian soup or pepper soup and been welcomed by an aroma you instantly recognized?
That unmistakable fragrance may be Nchuanwu known in English as scent leaf.
Scientifically called Ocimum gratissimum, Nchuanwu belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is also known as African basil, clove basil and wild basil.

 ONE PLANT, MANY NAMES
Among the Igbo, it is popularly called Nchuanwu/Nchanwu. The Yoruba call it Efirin, while other Nigerian communities have their own names.
 Native to Africa and widely distributed across tropical regions, this aromatic herb has become deeply connected to African food traditions.

 WHAT IS IT USED FOR?
Nchuanwu is primarily a culinary herb used to add fragrance and flavour. It can be used in pepper soup, traditional soups, stews, rice, beans, plantain and meat dishes.
Its secret is in its volatile essential oils, which can contain aromatic compounds such as eugenol, thymol and linalool. Crush the fresh leaves and their powerful aroma comes alive.

 NCHUANWU VS SWEET BASIL
They belong to the same Ocimum genus, but they aren't the same plant. Nchuanwu (Ocimum gratissimum) is often more pungent, with a distinctive clove like aroma.
Fresh leaves offer a vibrant aroma, while dried leaves provide convenience.
But Nchuanwu is more than an herb.
For many African families, its fragrance evokes home, mother's cooking, grandmother's soup and memories passed through generations.
One leaf. Many names. Many dishes. One beautiful African story.

text:
The New Industrial Supercycle Is Moving From Blueprints to Paychecks

Trump’s promised industrial supercycle is crossing from investment into production — and everything from GDP to factory payrolls is firing up.

Last month, the Enemedia crowed. The “experts” announced 1.5 percent growth and pronounced judgment. Trump’s promised boom had failed to arrive.

Wrong.

This month, the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model has third-quarter real growth running at a 4.7 percent annual rate.

As I told you then, the TDS crowd was looking at the wrong number. In the second quarter report, imports and inventories pulled the number down. But the import surge was led not by toys, trinkets, or flat-screen televisions, but by capital goods: telecommunications equipment, semiconductors, and industrial machinery.

The equipment American companies were importing to build the boom was temporarily concealing it. And right on schedule, those machines are now roaring to life.

Friday’s employment report did more than add 162,000 jobs. It showed the sequence I described last month moving into its next stage. Restaurants and local-government schools supplied much of the headline gain. But manufacturing payrolls rose by 16,000, nearly all of it in durable goods. Machinery and fabricated-metal producers accounted for 6,000 apiece, while construction gained another 22,000 jobs.

Even July’s reported loss of 23,000 jobs did not survive revision. It became a gain of 21,000. Manufacturing employment has now risen by 58,000 since December, while factory production workers are earning 4.4 percent more per hour than they were a year ago.

Indeed, the private sector has added 1.04 million jobs since Trump took office just a year and a half ago.

The industrial boom has begun to hire.

Investment Is Turning Into Production

The latest numbers tell the story. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers — the part of the economy powered by American consumers and private investment — grew at a 4.2 percent annual rate, up from the original 3.9 percent estimate. Equipment investment surged by 13.6 percent after rising 15.8 percent in the first quarter. 

Excluding the pandemic reopening, America has not seen back-to-back double-digit equipment-investment quarters in more than a decade.

Indeed, capital-goods imports jumped $14.4 billion, more than the entire $12 billion increase in goods imports. Computers, computer accessories, and semiconductors led the way. Yet through July, American exports were up 12 percent from the same period last year and the total trade deficit was down nearly 30 percent.

The private economy wasn’t standing still. It was buying productive capacity.

July’s trade figures show why the same buildout appears to depress GDP before it raises output. GDP subtracts an imported computer server from the trade component before the machine adds anything to American output. 

The same is true of a German machine tool or a Taiwanese chip-fabrication system. GDP counts where the machine was made when it arrives. Only later does it count what American workers make with it. A new plant necessarily increases construction spending and machinery orders well before the public sees its finished products or new paychecks.

But now that accounting lag is ending.

Core capital-goods shipments rose 1.2 percent in July. Through July, they were 8 percent above the same period last year. Machinery shipments jumped 2.9 percent for the month. The durable-goods backlog rose again to $1.6 trillion. The industrial-machinery figures were even stronger. Through July, orders were 39.5 percent above the same period last year; shipments were up 32.4 percent.

Those shipments are now becoming output. Durable-manufacturing output rose at an 8.9 percent annual rate in the second quarter. The August ISM report extends the pattern. Manufacturing expanded for an eighth straight month after ten months of contraction, and the production index reached 58.3.

The machines did what capital investment is supposed to do: they raised output faster than labor costs. Now the factories using them are adding people.

Inflation has not vanished, but it’s certainly getting better. Second-quarter core PCE inflation slowed from a 4.4 percent annual rate to 3.6 percent while private demand accelerated. 

Contrary to generations of Democrats, growth is not inflationary. Production is not the enemy of price stability: it is the means by which supply catches demand.

The Money to Keep Building

Industrial booms require financing, but the best financing is profitability. Profits are the financial capacity that funds capital spending, and Trump’s permanent business expensing contained in the One Big Beautiful Bill is driving growth by increasing the reward for putting that money to work now.

That’s no longer theoretical (it honestly never was). Current-production corporate profits rose 9.1 percent in the second quarter and 22.8 percent from a year earlier. Almost all of the quarterly increase came from domestic business.

Managements are clearly behaving like they expect the strength to last. The Wall Street Journal reports that companies raising current-quarter profit guidance outnumber those cutting it by nearly two to one.

Steve Moore calls this the biggest industrial boom in American history. Over the next quarter-century, he estimates $6 trillion to $7 trillion in AI and data-center investment alone, and two million to three million additional construction jobs. That’s a supercycle by any definition, and it’s just beginning.

Trump’s Plan Was Never Just a Tax Cut

As they do with his foreign policy, the political class keeps analyzing Trump’s economic program one policy at a time. That guarantees they will miss it until it slaps them in the face (and if the 1980s are any indication, they’ll deny it even then).

But the plan is a system. First come the trade agreements and investment commitments. Then land, permits, construction, equipment, workers, and suppliers. Production and exports follow.

Permanent tax cuts and full, immediate business expensing reward companies for building here, now. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calls the result a “CapEx boom in factories.” 

Massive deregulation — 129 regulations cut for every one new rule issued — shortens the time between deciding to build and opening the doors. Abundant energy powers everything. Defense expansion creates long production runs for some of the most advanced manufacturing on Earth.

Tariffs create leverage to open foreign markets, rebalance trade, and redirect supply chains away from China. Access to the world’s richest consumer market is exchanged for purchases, investment, and production inside the United States. And by exempting foreign companies from tariffs if they build plants here, the world is incentivized to create jobs in America and sell to its workers.

All these things helped Trump recruit more than $18 trillion in investment commitments. But Trump also traveled the world to pitch those deals and consistently came home with gold. No President has ever been more hands-on in building American jobs and the American future. And the new equipment and shipment figures show that the spending from those investments has begun.

The inevitability of deindustrialization was a lie. America deindustrialized due to bad policy decisions by both parties. It took draining the swamp to begin to rebuild America’s heartland.

Energy Powers the Supercycle

Energy is the machine underneath the machines.

EIA’s latest finalized data put U.S. crude production at 13.8 million barrels a day in June, after nearly touching 14 million in April. Petroleum exports — crude oil plus petroleum products — set a record 13.61 million barrels a day in April. May nearly matched it, while crude exports alone set a fresh monthly record of 5.73 million.

In 2008, America was “exporting” $700 billion a year to its enemies in exchange for their crude. Oh, how the tables have turned.

Total American energy exports reached a record 31 quadrillion Btu in 2025, while net energy exports rose 20 percent to another record. U.S. LNG shipments to Europe reached a record 10.3 billion cubic feet a day, up from 6.3 billion in 2024. The United States supplied 56 percent of the EU’s LNG imports in 2025, compared with a still-objectionable 13.9 percent from Russia.

All of that reflects simply enormous plant expansion, export income, and jobs. And the supply base is still expanding. EIA puts current peak U.S. natural-gas export capacity at 18.3 billion cubic feet a day. It expects total natural gas exports to grow by another 30 percent by 2027 as new terminals come online. 

Yet again, demand drives investment; investment builds factories and installs machinery; production and exports follow. That last bit is happening now.

April’s petroleum-export record came after disruption through Hormuz drove up global demand for American barrels. Export capacity can’t prevent a price shock. But supply outside the chokepoint offsets the disruption and keeps factories operating, both at home and abroad. 

The kind of global energy shock inflicted repeatedly by OPEC in the 1970s simply isn’t possible anymore.

Energy dominance is the foundation beneath the industrial supercycle — and one of America’s most powerful instruments of statecraft.

Defense Abroad Means Jobs At Home

Defense offers the clearest proof of how the process works. Through July, defense-capital-goods shipments were 28.7 percent above the same period last year; orders were up 43.3 percent.

Last month, I told you about Lockheed’s $65 billion in new orders and record $230 billion backlog. But then came the kind of commitment that turns a backlog into factories and jobs. 

A modification brought Lockheed’s seven-year PAC-3 multiyear agreement to $58.62 billion. Under the new contract, the company will triple PAC-3 capacity by the end of 2030, expanding its Camden, Arkansas plant by 50 percent. Lockheed plans to invest $9 billion through 2030 to modernize more than twenty U.S. facilities.

Previous administrations allowed U.S. shipbuilding to atrophy. But Trump’s on top of that too. Perhaps most striking is the new $76.6 billion award for five Columbia-class ballistic-missile submarines and nine Block VI Virginia-class guided missile submarines. 

As I explained last month, the long-lead contract matters every bit as much as the submarines themselves. It gives the private yards and their suppliers the certainty required to add production capacity, hire and train new workers, and build boats faster.

At the same time, the Navy announced a new multi-year contract with Raytheon to increase annual Tomahawk missile production from 68 to more than 1,000. That’s billions of dollars in new physical plant and skilled workers, and is just one example among many.

But contracts like this are only half the plan. The President’s separate August 13 memorandum orders plans for a fifth public Navy yard and a Component Repair Center stocked with complete “ship sets” of submarine spares.

Private yards build the fleet; public yards keep it at sea. America needs more of both.

Electric Boat’s 2026 goal is 8,000 hires across Connecticut and Rhode Island. HII reports that shipbuilding throughput rose 14 percent in 2025 and says it is targeting another 15 percent this year.

Five- to seven-year government commitments make those investments possible. A manufacturer cannot expand a plant, finance suppliers, qualify new sources, buy years of material, and train thousands of new and badly needed workers against one-off orders Congress may or may not renew. 

Long production runs turn demand into something a company can build against. They also greatly reduce the unit cost and the time to completion for the taxpayers.

You can’t command the seas with ships you can’t build, refuel, repair, or replace. Trump isn’t just buying missiles and submarines. He’s rebuilding the machine — and the workforce — that builds them.

I Told You This Was Coming

In February 2025, I wrote that Trump was turning America into the world’s energy powerhouse, using abundant oil and natural gas not merely to lower costs at home but to take markets from Russia and OPEC, supply our allies, strengthen the dollar, and turn trade negotiations into long-term orders for American energy.

Last July, when Congress made the Trump tax cuts and immediate business expensing permanent, I explained how the One Big Beautiful Bill would unleash purchases of plants and equipment that temporary provisions never could.

Then, in January, I went on Fox Business and NTD to predict the coming 2026 economic boom. I specifically pointed to the permanent tax cuts, Trump’s deregulatory offensive, $18 trillion in multi-year investment commitments, the reshoring of manufacturing, sharply higher defense spending, and the energy revolution.

I could list a hundred others, but the main point was always this: 1982 and 1983 were exactly the same. Real and permanent tax cuts spurred a surge in CapEx that slowly but surely transformed the economy. And in 1982 and 1983, the Enemedia breathlessly told us how the terrible economy and Reagan’s “trickle-down economics” (their term, not his), would result in his being a one-term President and leaving office in disgrace.

Yet he was right. And in 1984, he won 49 states.

So here we are again.

The Industrial Supercycle Is Hiring

Last month, I wrote:

"What we’re seeing right now is an order-book, equipment, construction, capacity, export, and productivity boom. Finished factories, full-rate production, broader hiring, and rising industrial wages come later. You don’t hire the entire operating workforce before building the plant. You don’t deliver the submarine before expanding the yard. And you don’t get the later output without making the earlier investment."

You didn’t in 1983 either.

Friday added the next link: payrolls. Factories are being built at an accelerating rate; the full fruit of that labor lies ahead. But orders are becoming shipments and output, and the industrial buildout has begun to hire.

For a generation, America’s ruling class told us manufacturing was gone forever. China would build; we would consume. Russia and the Middle East would supply the energy. Europe would regulate. America would borrow, import, and manage its inevitable decline.

Trump rejected every part of that foolishness.

The quiet boom is getting louder. The capital-goods surge that concealed it in August is now being followed by higher American production, lower unit costs, and new industrial paychecks. And the companies at the center of it have the profits and order books to keep building.

The Trump economic boom is here. But we’re still only seeing the leading edge of a Cat 5. The American industrial supercycle has begun.

ROBOTAXI

NEW TODAY
- Testers (stevenmarkryan): • Wild Tesla/Uber/Waymo Theory Just Dropped 😂
- Testers (TeslaZoa): According to the Tesla Robotaxi tracking site, 59 vehicles have been added to the fleet, bringing the total to 969. Only 31 more to go unti…
- Folder totals: Robotaxi 203 (+2) + Fleet 4 (0 new) → 207 unique
WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s paid autonomous ride service. You book a car in the Robotaxi app. The car drives. There is no human driver on unsupervised rides.
- Live cars today are mostly Model Y. The purpose-built Cybercab is the volume vehicle testers say Tesla is prioritizing.
- Camera-only vision. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy: no lidar, radar, or HD maps required for safe operation on this stack.
- This how-to merges the public Robotaxi service folder with Owning Robotaxi Fleet (owner / private-fleet economics). Not Cybercab-only bookmarks.

HOW IT WORKS
- Download the Tesla Robotaxi app and join the waitlist. Official robotaxi (Sep 2025): app is available to all; access expands over time.
- Book the ride in Tesla’s app. Elon: Tesla will not partner with Uber or Lyft. “We will have enough demand.”
- Unsupervised means no safety driver. Supervised cities still have a person in the car.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): service hours are 6am to 10pm, 7 days/week. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger. Upgraded vehicle distribution and routing so you wait less.
- Testers: you can change destination and keep the same trip for multiple stops.
- Cars return to a depot or homebase and park themselves (Houston footage).
- Ashok: FSD v15 is already running on Model Y robotaxis and will run on Cybercab.
- Testers: Tesla is limiting Model Y conversions to prioritize Cybercab, built with an unboxed modular process.
- Testers (Aug 24): Tesla expects Cybercab to replace Model Ys in the Robotaxi fleet over time and become the highest-volume vehicle there. Testers flag Sept 3 / 9/3 as the Cybercab strategy moment. Austin public Cybercab rides described as “imminent.”
- Testers (Sep 7): Cybercab expected to be actively deployed across Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet soon; Austin Cybercab wait times described as going parabolic on demand.
- Testers (Sep 7): Tesla hiring Robotaxi Fleet Support Supervisors night shift across 21 cities (Cybercabs incoming signal).
- Testers (Sep 7): Waymo Q3 2025 occupancy — 90% of trips have 2 or fewer people (two-seater Cybercab justification resurfaced).
- Testers (Sep 8): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 969 after +59 vehicles; 31 short of 1,000.

HOW TO USE
- Official robotaxi: download the app, join the waitlist.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): rides run 6am to 10pm every day. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; routing upgrade is meant to cut wait time.
- Testers: booking is in the app. One Orlando rider paid with an X Money card.
- Tesla site (as quoted): app in 29 languages; service animals; space for some wheelchairs and assistive devices.
- Testers: vehicles in Nevada must be marked “Robotaxi.”
- After the Aug 20 Nevada approval, testers say Tesla still has to finish vehicle inspections, insurance, and published rates before paid rides start there.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).
- Fleet / chamath: intends to buy and deploy large fleets nationally when possible; expects payback and positive FCF in under 2 years (tester / investor claim, not Official Tesla).
- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.
- Fleet / tslaming (Mar 2026): then only 8 unsupervised Austin robotaxis — historical; do not use as current fleet size (Robotaxi dump Aug 23 tester: 908 total).
- Testers / Teslaconomics (Aug 25, Robotaxi folder): “owning your own Tesla Robotaxi fleet can one day make you financially free.” Still a tester slogan — no Official owner-earnings number in this dump.
- CONFLICT / caution: owner earnings, Cybercab sticker, ROI, and payback are tester models. Dump explicitly says none of it is guaranteed. Do not treat as Official Tesla guidance.

SERVICE AREA / CITIES
- Unsupervised (no safety driver), as listed May 2026: Austin, TX (launched Jun 22, 2025); Dallas, TX and Houston, TX (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Supervised (safety driver), as listed May 2026: SF Bay Area, CA (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Testers: Bay Area rides to and from SFO. Earlier: San Jose Airport pickup.
- Testers: an Orlando rider reviewed a live Robotaxi trip (Jul 2026). Aug 21 testers also list Orlando and Tampa as live; that is not on the May 2026 official city list.
- Testers (Aug 25 Teslaconomics): 7 metro areas live. Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa ramping unsupervised; Bay Area still safety-driver. Treat as tester city list, not Official May 2026 list.
- Testers (Aug 27 travel_invest): recap of Official hours post lists 6 target cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa. Tester translation, not a new Official city list.
- Nevada (Aug 20, 2026): full network permit for paid public service. Start small in Clark County / Las Vegas; Tesla can expand elsewhere in the state after notifying the commission.
- Testers (Aug 23): Nevada approved Tesla for up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles, up from a 10-car interim limit. Tesla said it would be “extremely happy” to have around 2,500 running within a year.
- Testers (May 2026) said Tesla was also aiming at Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa.
- Hiring and test-vehicle posts (treat as signals, not live service): Arizona, Florida, Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, California, D.C., plus a Germany Arzfeld pilot with a safety driver and Japan Kanagawa job listings.
- Ashok: expanding to a new city is getting cheaper; the end state is operating whole states, not city by city.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- Official: Robotaxi app waitlist. Access expands as cities open.
- Testers (Aug 27 WorldlyReviewer): received an email from Tesla advertising Robotaxi. Tester report of Tesla marketing, not a new Official service announcement.
- Elon (Feb 2026): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Testers (JPMorgan via folder posts): robotaxi operating cost about $0.50–$0.60 per mile vs $2.50–$3.00 for typical ride-hail; long-term platform goal $0.30 per mile. Older Morgan Stanley note used $0.81 per mile vs Waymo $1.36–$1.43.
- Folder testers argue Tesla scales on existing Model Y / Cybercab manufacturing and Superchargers, vs lidar-heavy custom cars.
- Testers (Aug 23): Waymo’s latest self-driving hardware reportedly costs around $20K.
- See OWNING / FLEET for private-owner economics from the Owning Robotaxi Fleet folder.

SAFETY
- Elon: scale as fast as possible, but do not harm anyone. One injury becomes a worldwide headline and a regulatory clampdown.
- Ashok (Jul 2026): zero notable incidents over 380,000 unsupervised miles, across six cities in two states. Cameras only.
- Testers on NHTSA ADS data (Jun 16, 2025–Jul 15, 2026): zero collisions initiated by the Model Y ADS. Two new incidents were other drivers hitting a stopped or parked Robotaxi (Austin red-arrow stop; Dallas parked). No passengers, no injuries, no tow.
- Austin: testers said 100% of tracked robotaxi rides in that NHTSA window were unsupervised.
- Testers: 7x safer than the average human driver is an FSD claim in this folder, not a Robotaxi-only official stat.

FLEET AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; upgraded intelligence in vehicle distribution and routing. Testers (tslaming) say that gain is backend ops (demand forecasting, fleet placement), not a self-driving software change.
- Testers (Aug 23): 908 robotaxis in the total fleet. Treat as the latest tester count, not official.
- Testers (Aug 19): about 97 Cybercabs at the Houston Robotaxi lot. Model Ys and Cybercabs still rotating in the geofence.
- Testers: Tesla plans 80 wireless chargers in Austin as Phase 2 of a Robotaxi charging hub.
- Testers: private (not public) V4 Supercharger depots, including 56 stalls in Chandler / Phoenix East Valley; a Dallas-area fleet depot; a Las Vegas Cybercab wash/service site.
- Testers: scale needs charging, cleaning, and maintenance automated, not only FSD.
- Fleet-size tweets in this folder are days-to-months apart and disagree. Do not treat an old 500–600 car count (or the Mar 2026 “8 unsupervised in Austin” fleet-folder snapshot) as current.

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- New city: download the Robotaxi app, join the waitlist, ride when your city opens.
- Live city: book in the Tesla app. Try a multi-stop trip if the app offers it.
- Airport: testers already used SFO and SJC where those pickups were live.
- Watch Nevada: paid Las Vegas service after the Aug 20 permit plus leftover admin steps; testers now cite a 5,000-vehicle cap.
- Watch Austin: testers say public Cybercab rides are “imminent.”
- Owning a fleet: not open as a turnkey product in this dump. Watch Elon’s owner-network comments + Tesla fee structure; treat $30k/yr and <2yr payback as tester models only.
